planting.note: Set container-grown divisions in spring once soil is workable, spacing them to let the dark rosettes fill in without crowding.

directions: Xenox is a compact Sunsparkler-series selection prized for foliage that emerges deep plum and matures to nearly black through the growing season, topped by cherry-red flower clusters in late summer. Grow in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; the darkest leaf color and sturdiest stems develop with at least six hours of direct sun daily. Avoid rich or consistently moist soil, which encourages floppy growth and crown rot. Divide clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor and a tight mounded habit.
sources: Proven Winners Sunsparkler Sedum series information

common_name: Chocolate Drop Sedum (Dwarf Chocolate-Brown Foliage Stonecrop)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring toward the front of a bed or rock garden where the low, chocolate-toned foliage can be seen up close.

directions: Chocolate Drop is one of the shortest Sunsparkler cultivars, forming a dense low mound of rich chocolate-brown, glossy leaves that hold their color through the season and turn deep bronze-red in autumn. Small clusters of rose-pink starry flowers open in late summer just above the foliage, drawing bees and butterflies. Plant in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; it makes an excellent edging or rock-garden plant and tolerates heat and drought once established. Excess moisture or shade will cause the compact habit to stretch and lose its rich leaf color.
sources: Proven Winners Sunsparkler Sedum series information

common_name: Karfunkelstein Sedum (Deep Burgundy Foliage Upright Stonecrop)

planting.note: Divide and transplant in early spring into well-drained border soil where the dark foliage can contrast with silver or chartreuse companions.

directions: Karfunkelstein is a German-bred border stonecrop with fleshy, deep burgundy-purple foliage that darkens further through summer, contrasting with clustered heads of dusky rose-pink flowers in early fall. It performs best in lean to average, well-drained soil in full sun, where strong light intensifies the leaf pigmentation and keeps stems upright and self-supporting. Overly rich or wet soil promotes weak, sprawling growth and increases the risk of crown rot. Leave the dried seed heads standing through winter for structural interest and to feed overwintering birds.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Install spring divisions in full sun and lean soil; give plants room to form a full clump before flower heads open in late summer.

directions: Neon is a showy stonecrop selection valued for its unusually intense magenta-pink, flat-topped flower clusters that appear from late summer into fall above broad, succulent grey-green leaves. It thrives in lean to moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and shrugs off heat, drought, and poor soil once established. As with other border sedums, wet or overly rich conditions cause floppy growth and are the main cause of failure. Leave spent flower heads in place over winter for seasonal texture and to support pollinators and seed-eating birds.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in a spot with reliable drainage; watch for occasional all-green reversion shoots and remove them to preserve variegation.

directions: Frosty Morn is grown chiefly for its striking foliage, with blue-green succulent leaves broadly edged in creamy white, giving the whole plant a frosted appearance from spring through frost. Loose clusters of pale pink to white flowers appear in late summer, though the variegated foliage remains the main attraction all season. It tolerates a bit more shade than typical border stonecrops but still needs well-drained soil to avoid rot, and stems can be lax so light staking or growing among neighboring perennials helps keep the clump tidy. Divide every few years to maintain strong variegation and prevent the center of the clump from thinning.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Class Act Sedum (Sturdy Upright Rose-Red Stonecrop)

planting.note: Set divisions in full sun in spring; the sturdy stems rarely need staking even in exposed border sites.

directions: Class Act was bred for a strongly upright, non-flopping habit, holding its rounded heads of rose-red flowers well above tidy blue-green foliage from late summer into fall. Grow in full sun and lean, well-drained soil, where the reinforced stems remain self-supporting through wind and rain far better than older upright sedum cultivars. It is drought tolerant once established and needs little supplemental feeding; excess nitrogen encourages soft, weaker growth. Leave the seed heads standing through winter for garden structure and to feed birds before cutting back in early spring.
